title: CEM orientation, exam strategy & energy-manager role
outcome: Understand the exam, reference strategy, energy-management process and how this course works.
teaching_points: The exam is open-book, but open-book is not the same as unlimited time. The skill is fast recognition: know what the question is asking, know which reference family contains the answer, and avoid spending several minutes searching.

Use a two-pass strategy. First answer questions you can solve or locate quickly. Mark slow calculations and uncertain theory for the second pass. A 4-hour/130-question exam averages about 1.85 minutes per question, so time must be actively managed.
The energy-manager role is system-level: establish a baseline, identify opportunities, quantify savings and cost, implement, verify, maintain, and communicate results.

title: Energy, power, units & dimensional thinking
outcome: Build the unit foundation used across tariffs, HVAC, electrical, steam and economics.
teaching_points: Energy is the ability to do work; power is the rate at which energy is used or transferred. kW is power, kWh is energy. Confusing them is one of the most damaging basic errors.
Dimensional thinking is a safety system. Before calculating, write units beside every value. Units should cancel to the requested answer.
Core SI conversions used repeatedly include 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ and 1 W = 1 J/s. Learn to move comfortably among W, kW, MW, kWh, MJ and GJ.

title: Climate change, decarbonization & clean-energy transition
outcome: Understand decarbonization language, policy drivers, electrification and transition concepts.
teaching_points: Decarbonization means reducing greenhouse-gas emissions associated with energy and other activities. Energy efficiency usually comes early because reducing demand makes later electrification and renewable supply smaller and cheaper.
Electrification shifts end uses from direct fuel combustion to electricity. Its climate benefit depends on equipment efficiency and the emissions intensity of the electricity supply.
Clean-energy transition questions are often conceptual: identify the measure that reduces emissions, improves resilience, or supports a lower-carbon energy system.

title: Sustainability, SDGs, ESG/CSR & circular economy
outcome: Differentiate sustainability frameworks and their energy-management implications.
teaching_points: Sustainability balances environmental, economic and social outcomes rather than focusing only on energy cost.

The UN SDGs are broad development goals; ESG is a framework used by organizations/investors to assess environmental, social and governance performance; CSR concerns corporate responsibility and conduct.
Circular-economy thinking aims to reduce material and energy waste by keeping products/materials in use, recovering value and designing out waste.

title: GHG accounting, carbon footprints & net-zero logic
outcome: Understand Scope logic, carbon-accounting structure and basic carbon calculations.
teaching_points: GHG inventories separate emissions by organizational and operational boundaries. Scope 1 is direct emissions from owned/controlled sources; Scope 2 is purchased energy; Scope 3 covers other value-chain emissions.
A carbon calculation is usually activity data multiplied by an emissions factor. Keep units explicit: e.g., kWh × kg CO2e/kWh.
Net zero does not mean zero energy use. It means balancing residual emissions with removals/credible neutralization after deep reductions, according to the applicable framework.

title: Codes, standards, green buildings & resilience
outcome: Know what major standards/frameworks are for and avoid confusing their scopes.
teaching_points: Treat standards as a map of purpose. ASHRAE 90.1 is energy efficiency for buildings except low-rise residential; 62.1 addresses ventilation/IAQ; 135 is BACnet; Guideline 14 concerns measurement of energy/demand savings; 211 addresses commercial-building energy audits.

ISO 50001 is an energy-management-system standard. LEED is a green-building rating system. ENERGY STAR provides benchmarking/rating tools. IEEE 519 addresses harmonic control at the point of common coupling.
Do not memorize every clause. For CEM preparation, first master what each document is for, when it applies, and how it differs from nearby distractors.

title: Energy rates and utility-bill anatomy
outcome: Read energy, demand and fixed-charge components and translate billing units.
teaching_points: A utility bill can contain energy charges, demand charges, fixed/customer charges, taxes, fuel adjustments, power-factor provisions and time-of-use pricing.
Energy charges depend on consumption over time; demand charges depend on the highest measured or billed demand during a defined interval.
Always separate the bill into components before calculating. Do not multiply kWh by a demand rate or kW by an energy rate.

title: Demand, load factor, ratchets & peak management
outcome: Calculate load factor/ratchets and understand peak-demand reduction.
teaching_points: Load factor compares average demand with peak demand over the same period. A low load factor means the peak is high relative to average use.
A demand ratchet can keep billed demand high even when current measured demand falls. Compute the ratchet minimum and compare it with actual demand.
Peak management focuses on when loads occur. Efficiency may reduce both kWh and kW, while load shifting can reduce kW without necessarily reducing total kWh.

title: Fuel pricing, point-of-use cost & supply comparison
outcome: Compare fuels/electricity on delivered-energy basis including efficiency.
teaching_points: Fuel comparison must be made on a common useful-energy basis. First convert all fuels to the same energy unit; then account for end-use efficiency.
A cheaper fuel per unit of purchased energy can still be more expensive at the point of use if conversion efficiency is poor.
HHV/LHV basis matters. Use the basis provided by the problem/reference and do not mix them silently.

outcome: Understand audit depth, workflow, data needs and energy-management measures.
teaching_points: An energy audit progresses from understanding the facility and bills to field investigation, measurement, analysis and recommendations.

A good EEM is not merely an idea. It defines the baseline, proposed change, expected savings, cost, interactions, assumptions and verification approach.

outcome: Select instruments for electrical, temperature, IR, light, combustion and heat measurements.
teaching_points: Instrument selection begins with the physical quantity: voltage/current/power, temperature, infrared radiation, illuminance, combustion gases or heat flow.

Infrared cameras show surface-temperature patterns, not hidden heat directly. Emissivity, reflections and line of sight affect interpretation.

title: EUI, ECI, load factor, HHV/LHV & audit KPIs
outcome: Calculate and interpret common audit KPIs and fuel bases.
teaching_points: EUI normalizes annual energy use by floor area; ECI normalizes annual energy cost by area. They are screening/benchmarking metrics, not complete explanations of performance.
Facility load factor = actual energy / (peak demand × period hours). Keep the time period consistent.
HHV includes the heat associated with condensing water vapor; LHV excludes it. Never compare efficiency or fuel values across mixed bases.

Digital tools accelerate analysis, but the energy manager remains responsible for data quality, reasonableness and engineering judgment.

title: Cash-flow basics, simple payback & project screening
outcome: Translate energy savings into annual cash flow and simple payback.
teaching_points: Simple payback = investment / net annual savings. It is fast and intuitive but ignores cash flows after payback and the time value of money.
Translate technical savings into annual money: energy savings × energy rate, demand savings × demand rate, plus/minus O&M impacts.
Use simple payback for screening, not as the only criterion for long-lived projects.

outcome: Choose and compute discounted-cash-flow measures.

title: SIR, IRR and life-cycle-cost comparisons
outcome: Interpret and solve SIR/IRR/LCC style decisions.
teaching_points: SIR = PV savings / PV costs; values above 1 indicate discounted savings exceed discounted costs under the assumptions.
IRR is the discount rate at which NPV becomes zero. It can be found by financial functions, trial-and-error or interpolation.
Life-cycle cost includes relevant costs over the study period, not just first cost. Compare alternatives on a common economic basis.

Straight-line depreciation spreads depreciable basis across useful life under the stated assumptions. Tax effects depend on the problem's rules.
Exam traps often arise from mixing nominal and real rates, using gross rather than net savings, or double-counting escalation.

outcome: Understand real/reactive/apparent power before PF calculations.

Low PF increases current and kVA for the same real kW, increasing upstream losses/capacity requirements.

title: Power factor and capacitor correction
outcome: Calculate existing PF relationships and required capacitor kVAR.

Correcting PF does not materially reduce the real kW needed to produce the same shaft work; it mainly reduces current/kVA/reactive flow.

teaching_points: Induction-motor slip is the difference between synchronous speed and actual rotor speed. Slip increases with load.

Rewinding may affect efficiency depending on quality; compare life-cycle cost, reliability and verified efficiency rather than assuming new or rewound is always best.

title: ESPC structures: guaranteed/shared savings, PDA and UESC
outcome: Differentiate performance-contract structures and risk allocation.
teaching_points: ESPCs use verified energy/cost savings to support project economics. Guaranteed-savings structures typically place more performance risk on the ESCO while the customer finances/repays; shared-savings structures share realized savings under contract terms.
Project development agreements define development responsibilities before a full performance contract. UESCs are utility-facilitated mechanisms in relevant jurisdictions.
Contract questions often test risk allocation, guarantee, ownership, financing and M&V responsibilities.

title: M&V fundamentals and savings/avoided-cost logic
outcome: Understand baseline, adjustments and verification principles.
teaching_points: M&V compares performance against a baseline while accounting for changes that would have affected energy use.
Savings are not directly measured because the baseline after retrofit is counterfactual. A common form is savings = adjusted baseline use - reporting-period use.
Routine adjustments use expected independent variables; non-routine adjustments address structural changes such as area, equipment or operating conditions.
